tagline.text: A Catanduanes surf beach where Pacific swells peel into a right-hand barrel

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Feb–Jun for beginners and sightseeing, Jul–Oct for big waves

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000–2,500 (per day, covering lodging, meals, lessons and transport; flights excluded)

children.text: Puraran Beach is a surf beach on the east coast of Catanduanes in Baras, known for "Majestics," a right-hand barrel formed where Pacific swells hit the coral reef. When the waves are small you can take beginner lessons, and you can add the sunrise at nearby Binurong Point and a few waterfalls.

Puraran is a small village in the municipality of Baras on the east side of Catanduanes, with a beach about a mile long. It faces the Pacific head-on, so swells from across the ocean arrive directly, and the right-hand wave that breaks on the reef about 200 m offshore is known among surfers as "Majestics." The beach is framed by high cliffs and rocks, the sand is fine, and mountains rise right behind it, giving the place a rugged feel.

Majestics is a thick, hollow right-hand barrel, and at 6 feet and above it is described as powerful enough to snap boards. That makes the beach a spot for intermediate to advanced surfers in the big-swell months, and a place to practice near the shore with an instructor when the waves are small. Sources disagree on who named the wave and when it was discovered: one account says a Hawaiian photographer named it in 1986 while on assignment for a surf magazine, and another says it became known in the late 1970s.

Puraran is not a swimming beach. Several travelers report that the waves are too strong to swim out comfortably. Slow-paced activities suit it better: surf lessons, beach walks, nearby viewpoints, waterfalls and watching the sunrise. The resorts sit in a small cluster along the beach and most guests eat at their lodging, so it works well for surfers and travelers who want to stay quietly for a few days.

Catanduanes is hit by typhoons often and is nicknamed the "Land of the Howling Winds." The same typhoons generate the swells that build Puraran's waves, so the surf season overlaps with typhoon risk. Plan with some slack, and keep an eye on weather forecasts and flight and ferry updates.
This thick right-hander breaks over the reef, and on big days it forms barrels that run for tens of meters. Because it breaks about
offshore, you can watch surfers appear small against the swell from the beach. The bottom is coral, so even advanced surfers need to be careful here.
When the waves are small, you can take beginner lessons with a local instructor in the inside section of the beach. Lessons are reported at about
per hour, board included. On big days, stay out of Majestics and practice only in the area your instructor picks.

Puraran opens to the east, so the sun rises straight out of the horizon at dawn. Cliffs on both sides of the beach and limestone rocks just offshore shape the view, and the sand is fine but gritty rather than powdery. On days when the surf is strong, watching from the water's edge is a show in itself.
Binurong Point
is a grassy hill you reach from Puraran by motorbike, and the Pacific opens up after an easy walk of about
20–30 minutes
from the entrance. For sunrise, set out in the early dark; an entrance fee, an environmental fee and a guide fee are charged separately.
Balacay Point in Baras has no entrance fee, and a paved road runs close to the summit. It is described as a tricycle ride from Puraran followed by a walk of about
15–20 minutes
uphill. Go before sunset for fewer people and better views.
Ba-Haw Falls is near Puraran, and Nahulugan Falls lies north of Baras; Nahulugan is described as about
1 hour
away by motorbike. Your resort can arrange a guide, or you can rent a motorbike and go on your own.

Using Puraran as a base makes other sights on Catanduanes easy to reach. Bato Church, Sakahon Beach and Maribina Falls are the best known. Motorbike rental is rare around Puraran, so it is common to rent in Virac or charter a vehicle for the day.

Drop your bags at your lodging and have lunch. There is no ATM in Puraran, so withdraw cash in Virac beforehand.
Take a beginner lesson in the inside section, or on big days watch the surfers at Majestics. The reef is shallow, so bring reef boots and a rash guard.
Watch the sunset at Balacay Point and head back to your lodging.
The next morning, leave before dawn for Binurong Point to see the sunrise. Come back for breakfast, pack up and head out to Virac.

If your return flight is in the morning, it is safer to go out to Virac the day before and sleep there. Buses and vans between Puraran and Virac Airport run infrequently, so ask your lodging about the last departure first.

items.title: 4 days 3 nights: surf focus
items.subtitle: A mix of lessons and island drives

children.text: Arrive in Puraran, rest at your lodging, then take a beach walk and watch the sunset.
Take a surf lesson in the morning and relax at the hammocks or on the beach in the afternoon. Early mornings tend to have lighter wind and cleaner wave shape.
Rent a motorbike or car and tour the south of the island, including Bato Church, Sakahon Beach and Maribina Falls.
See the sunrise at Binurong Point before dawn, then take a morning bus or van to Virac and catch your flight home.
If surfing is the goal, plan around the size of the waves at Majestics. Use small-wave days as rest days, and on big days it is fine just to watch.
Cebu Pacific flies from Manila (MNL) to Virac Airport (VRC) about once a day (2026 timetables; it is the only nonstop carrier), and the flight is described as taking about
1 hour
. Fares can be high, so many travelers watch for promos and seat sales.
Flight days and times change by season. Check the airline's announcements before you book.

depending on seat class, so check current fares at the terminal.
The ferry from Tabaco Port to San Andres or Virac on Catanduanes takes about
3–5 hours
, with fares reported at about
for ordinary seats and about
for air-conditioned seats (2026 operator and fare sites disagree, so this is a range, and fuel surcharges may push it higher). Sailings can be delayed or canceled by weather and waves.
From the port, continue to Puraran by van or tricycle.
Ferry schedules change often, and some operators do not take online bookings. Check on site at Tabaco Port.
Baras town is about
24km
from Virac, and Puraran takes about
1–1.5 hours
by van, bus or jeepney.
Vans and jeepneys heading east wait in front of Virac Port and leave when full. The van is reported at about
per person and the bus at about
Chartering a tricycle from Baras to Puraran is reported at about
There are only a few buses a day. Ask your lodging for the current schedule.
You can walk between the beach and the resorts in Puraran. For Binurong Point or Balacay Point, take a motorbike taxi or a tricycle.
Motorbike rental is scarce around Puraran. One lodging in Baras has been reported renting them for about
per day, and in Virac you can rent at a similar rate.

The best time to visit depends on your purpose. Surfers who want to watch or ride big waves are told to come in July–October, when Pacific swells arrive, and some sources say September–October is the strongest. Beginners and intermediates do better in February–June, when the waves are smaller.
From November to January, onshore winds often spoil the waves and rain is frequent. This period suits relaxing more than surfing.
Catanduanes is often affected by typhoons. From July to November, check the weather forecast and leave some slack on your return day in case flights and ferries stop.

Puraran has small surfer-oriented lodgings along the beach, including Majestic Puraran Beach Resort, Puraran Surf Resort, Puraran Wahine Surf Retreat and Titaay's Surf Haus. Options include cottages, dorms and regular rooms, with prices varying by season and facilities. Many places also arrange surf lessons, board rental and tours. Foreign surfers fill the lodgings in the surf season, so book ahead for July–October.

Most guests eat at their lodging, and many places serve Bicolano dishes cooked with seafood and coconut milk. There are few shops nearby, so it helps to buy water and snacks in Virac beforehand; options shrink the farther you travel from Virac toward Baras. Withdraw cash in Virac too.
There is no ATM in Puraran and few options in Baras. Withdraw plenty of cash in Virac.
The beach bottom is a sharp coral reef. Wear reef boots when you surf, and because the sun is strong, wear a rash guard or a long-sleeve top.
Majestics is described as a wave for intermediate surfers and above. Beginners should practice only in the inside section chosen by a local instructor.
Surf lessons are reported at about
per hour with a board. Rates differ by resort, so confirm before you book.
The Binurong Point sunrise requires a pre-dawn start. The walk from the entrance to the top takes about
20–30 minutes
, so wear non-slip shoes.
Mobile signal is weak or absent in many places. Save maps offline and confirm your bookings in advance.
Typhoons are frequent here. From July to November, check flight and ferry operations and plan a spare day on your return.
Bus and van schedules are irregular. Ask your lodging about the last departure toward Virac.
The coral-reef bottom and strong rip currents at Puraran can be dangerous even for experienced surfers. On big-wave days it is safest to stay out of the water.
Strong rips and undertow can form in the sea off the beach. Swim only on calm days and in areas where locals advise it is safe.
The reef is shallow, so a fall can cause cuts or serious injury. Protect both your board and your body.
In the big-wave season the surf is described as powerful enough to break boards. Check the condition of any gear you rent.

When a typhoon makes landfall, flights and ferries stop and roads can be blocked. Typhoon Uwan (Fung-wong) badly damaged Catanduanes seaports in November 2025 (operations resumed on 11 November), and Tropical Storm Ada brought heavy rain and flooding to Catanduanes again in January 2026. I could not confirm the current operating status of Puraran lodgings, so ask before booking, and prepare travel insurance and a flexible schedule.
Entrance fees and guide rules at Binurong Point and Balacay Point can change, so check the latest announcements.
